strengths: The proposed method is a non-invasive post-processing framework that does not interfere with the core training of Gaussian Splatting, making it easy to integrate with existing pipelines.
Projecting training-view errors and visibilities back onto the Gaussian primitives and rendering them as 2D feature maps for downstream regression is an intuitive and geometrically sound concept.
The paper provides a very thorough evaluation, including in-scene and out-of-scene generalization, object-centric vs. full-scene analysis, and a detailed step-wise backward feature selection study.
The proposed approach achieves significant improvements over the main baseline (FisherRF) across multiple datasets in terms of both Pearson correlation and AUSE.
weaknesses: A major limitation is the reliance on holdout data with ground truth (color and/or depth) to train the regression models (even if it is just a single view). This stands in contrast to zero-shot or training-free uncertainty methods (like standard FisherRF) that do not require any target error maps to define uncertainty.

The computational and memory overhead of storing up to 13 additional features per Gaussian primitive (some encoded with spherical harmonics) and rendering these multiple maps is not quantitatively discussed. This is particularly important for real-time applications where 3DGS is typically preferred.

The evaluation datasets (LF and TUM SLAM) are mostly object-centric and relatively small-scale. Testing the method on larger, unbounded scenes (such as the Mip-NeRF 360 dataset) would show how well the proposed feature projection scales to complex backgrounds and large depth ranges.

strengths: The core idea of projecting empirical training errors and visibilities back onto the 3D Gaussian primitives to construct rendering-based uncertainty features is highly intuitive, elegant, and novel.
Being a post-processing method, it does not interfere with standard 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) training, making it easily applicable to pre-trained models.

The evaluation is quite thorough, testing on multiple datasets (Light Field and TUM RGB-D SLAM), depth vs. rendering error, in-scene vs. out-of-scene generalization, and full-scene vs. object-centric settings.

The step-wise backward feature selection study is very insightful and helps identify which rendered feature maps (e.g., FoV counter, visibility under different aggregations) are most informative for estimating uncertainty.
weaknesses: The method requires computing and storing reconstruction errors across all training views to build the error representations ($E(k)$ and $E^*(k,\vec{d})$), which introduces additional computational and storage overhead.

For in-scene uncertainty estimation, the method requires holdout views with ground truth to train the regression model (e.g., gradient boosting). While the authors show that out-of-scene generalization is moderately successful without target-scene holdout data, there is still a noticeable performance drop in that setting.
Comparison with other recent uncertainty estimation methods for 3DGS (such as Bayesian/stochastic approaches or active learning variants) is somewhat limited beyond the FisherRF baseline.

There are several minor typos throughout the manuscript that should be corrected, such as 'oppacity' (page 1), 'trainings views' (page 1), 'Ituitively' (page 7), and 'compleat' (page 7, caption of Figure 2).

strengths: Novel and intuitive pipeline that projects training errors and visibility back onto 3D Gaussian primitives, rendering them to novel views to serve as multi-channel uncertainty features for regression.

Comprehensive evaluation on two benchmark datasets (Light Field and TUM RGB-D) for both depth error and rendering error estimation, showing consistent improvements over standard baselines like FisherRF.
Detailed ablation studies, including a greedy backward feature selection analysis to evaluate the importance of different constructed feature maps (e.g., FoV counter, visibility maps).
Exploration of both in-scene and out-of-scene generalization scenarios, providing useful insights into the transferability of the learned regression models.
weaknesses: Dependency on Holdout Views: The in-scene model requires holdout views with ground truth to train the pixel-wise regression model. Reserving views for this purpose directly reduces the data available for training the 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) model itself. The paper lacks a quantitative analysis of this trade-off (i.e., how much 3DGS reconstruction quality degrades when reserving views for training the uncertainty regressor).

Out-of-Scene Performance Drop: When generalizing to completely unseen scenes (Table 4), the performance of the regressor drops significantly (e.g., Pearson correlations dropping to ~0.3-0.5 for rendering error). This indicates that the feature-to-error mapping is still heavily scene-dependent, limiting practical out-of-scene deployment.

Lack of Efficiency and Overhead Analysis: The proposed method requires storing 13 additional features (some direction-dependent using Spherical Harmonics) per Gaussian primitive, rendering 13 separate feature maps per novel view, and running a gradient boosting regressor. There is no discussion or quantitative measurement of the training time, inference/rendering speed (FPS), or memory overhead compared to vanilla 3DGS or FisherRF.

Counter-intuitive Spatial Interaction Results: In Section 4, the authors state that incorporating spatial context via CNNs did not outperform pixel-wise gradient boosting. Since rendering and depth errors are highly structured and spatially correlated, one would expect a convolutional model to perform better. The failure of the CNNs suggests either sub-optimal tuning or that the projected pixel-wise features lack sufficient structural consistency.

Dense and Confusing Mathematical Notations: Equations (4) through (8) are highly dense and introduce custom aggregation functions that are difficult to follow. Clarifying the physical intuition and the exact pixel-to-primitive mapping process would significantly improve readability.

strengths: Proposes a novel, elegant, and purely post-hoc uncertainty estimation (UE) framework for 3D Gaussian Splatting (GS) without requiring retraining or altering the initial optimization.

Introduces a clever 3D primitive-level projection scheme that maps training-view reconstruction errors and coverage statistics directly onto Gaussian primitives, which can then be rendered to form multi-channel uncertainty feature maps.

Demonstrates impressive performance improvements in both rendering (RGB) and depth uncertainty estimation over state-of-the-art baselines (e.g., FisherRF, BayesRays, var3DGS) across multiple datasets.

Shows a highly practical application to Active View Selection (AVS), outperforming existing approaches by directly leveraging the proposed direction-dependent coverage representations without needing to train the downstream regression model.

Provides a thorough evaluation, including scene separation (foreground/background), out-of-scene generalization, step-wise feature importance studies, and an exploration of spatial context using CNNs.
weaknesses: Requires at least one or a few holdout views (with ground-truth target color/depth errors) to train the pixel-wise gradient-boosting meta-regressor, which might limit deployment in fully zero-shot scenarios where no validation viewpoints are available.

The accumulation and rendering of 13 separate primitive-level features (especially the direction-dependent ones represented with spherical harmonics) introduce extra memory and computation overhead. Quantifying the exact runtime and storage cost compared to vanilla GS would make the practical analysis more complete.

strengths: Presents a novel and elegant post-hoc framework (PRIMU) for uncertainty estimation in Gaussian Splatting without requiring any modifications to the initial training or optimization process.
Proposes a clever feature-representation concept where historical training-view errors and coverage statistics are projected onto 3D Gaussian primitives and rendered as 2D feature maps.

Exhibits superior performance over current state-of-the-art methods (such as FisherRF, var3DGS, manifold, and BayesRays) in both rendering and depth uncertainty estimation across multiple diverse datasets.
Demonstrates the practical utility of the proposed features for Active View Selection (AVS), successfully improving novel view synthesis quality under tight view budgets.

Provides a thorough set of evaluations, including detailed feature-combination studies, scene-separation analysis (foreground vs. background), and generalization experiments in the supplementary materials.
weaknesses: Dependency on hold-out data: The framework requires at least one hold-out view with ground truth (RGB or depth) to train the meta-regressor. While the authors show the model can generalize across scenes, this remains a limitation compared to purely self-contained/zero-shot uncertainty estimation methods.

Memory and Storage Overhead: Storing 13 different features per Gaussian primitive (with some being direction-dependent and encoded via spherical harmonics up to degree four) can drastically increase the memory footprint of the scene representation.

Lack of runtime and computational complexity analysis: The paper does not report quantitative benchmarks regarding the time and memory overhead required to generate, render (running the rasterizer for multiple feature maps), and run pixel-wise gradient boosting regression. This is crucial for applications in safety-critical robotics where real-time performance is necessary.

strengths: Highly innovative post-hoc uncertainty estimation framework for 3D Gaussian Splatting that maps training-view errors and coverage statistics back onto the 3D Gaussian primitives.

Achieves significant performance improvements (lower AUSE and much higher Pearson correlation) over existing state-of-the-art methods like FisherRF, var3DGS, and BayesRays for both color and depth uncertainty.
The proposed method is purely post-hoc and does not degrade the rendering quality of the underlying 3D-GS model, which is a major advantage over stochastic-based methods.

Comprehensive evaluation across multiple standard datasets (LF, LLFF, MipNeRF360, TUM) and detailed analysis, including feature selection ablation, foreground-background separation, and generalization to unseen scenes.
Demonstrates strong practical utility in Active View Selection (AVS), outperforming existing baselines in final reconstruction quality.
weaknesses: The meta-regression step requires at least one hold-out view with ground-truth data (color or depth) to train/calibrate the pixel-wise regressor. While the authors demonstrate some generalization to unseen scenes in the supplementary material, this dependency limits applicability in fully zero-shot settings where no ground-truth is available for a new scene.
The paper lacks discussion on the computational and memory overhead of the post-hoc stage, specifically the projection of training-view errors and coverage statistics onto the 3D primitives.

The connection between the active view selection (AVS) strategy and the main PRIMU pipeline is slightly loose, as the AVS approach completely omits the regression model and relies solely on a single coverage feature map.
